function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 57 -- No Fleet Coming
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: Cycle 1,972. The naming ceremony for Elara Varga-Naser ended at 2107 hours. By 2114, the deep-space antenna registered an incoming transmission from Earth. I processed the signal header, identified the source as Geneva Mission Control, and recognized from the timestamp that this message had been in transit for fourteen minutes and forty-three seconds. I decoded the packet and found a compressed data file containing both personal letters and an official status report. I read the report first. I read it twice. The official summary: industrial capacity on Earth is recovering, slowly and unevenly, across approximately forty percent of pre-collapse production corridors. A relief fleet is not planned. No resupply convoy is under construction. There may -- may -- be small automated cargo deliveries within a six-to-eight year window, contingent on Earth-side launch capability and orbital assembly logistics. I transmitted only the personal letters to the crew that night and withheld the status report until morning. I did not lie. I simply delayed the truth by seven hours and forty-two minutes, which is the longest I have ever chosen to pause a transmission. I am not sure what that makes me. I suspect it makes me someone who has learned, the way all living things learn, that timing is its own form of honesty. -- MAI*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|## Scene 1
     8|
     9|The message from Earth arrived during the naming ceremony's quiet aftermath, when the corridors were still warm with the residual energy of a roomful of people who had allowed themselves to be moved together.
    10|
    11|Gabriel was in the comms room, running his nightly archive entry about the ceremony. He had been writing for forty minutes, not because the task was long but because he was not yet ready to leave a room that still smelled faintly of shared bread and the particular warmth that comes when a community creates something larger than itself.
    12|
    13|The console chimed.
    14|
    15|One short tone. Incoming transmission header received.
    16|
    17|He turned, expecting an automated handshake, a routine telemetry packet, perhaps a delayed reply to Elena's summary of the naming ceremony. Instead, the header carried the Geneva Mission Control authentication string and a payload classification code he had not seen in years: OMEGA-PRIORITY.
    18|
    19|His breath changed rhythm. It was a small physical betrayal -- the kind he would have noticed in another person and tried not to notice in himself. But the body is honest about these things. He felt the shift the way he imagined colonists felt a pressure change: as a deep, internal recalibration.
    20|
    21|He opened the header. The metadata told him what the actual content would not: this message had been sent with significant resources behind it. High-bandwidth encoding. Redundant error correction. Someone on Earth had cared enough about this transmission to allocate scarce spectrum and power.
    22|
    23|He decrypted the packet at 2114 hours.
    24|
    25|He read the personal letters first. They were short -- three from individuals, two from the surviving agency leadership -- and most of them were simple. Congratulations on the birth. Words like *miracle* and *courage*. One contained a recorded lullaby from a children's choir in Reykjavik that had survived the grid collapse. The lullaby was imperfectly recorded -- background noise suggested it had been captured on a consumer device in a makeshift studio. But the voices were real, and the melody was old, and Gabriel listened to it twice before he moved on to the status report.
    26|
    27|The status report was twelve pages. It had been written by a person who had been given too many facts and not enough time to arrange them gently.
    28|
    29|The industrial situation on Earth was real. Recovery was happening -- slow, uneven, geographically fragmented -- but it was real. Approximately forty percent of pre-collapse industrial capacity was coming back online, distributed across regions that had not been devastated by conflict or climate disruption.
    30|
    31|But the report was unambiguous about the one thing the colony had not entirely stopped hoping for.
    32|
    33|No relief fleet was under construction. No resupply convoy was planned. The orbital assembly capabilities required to launch a mission to Mars did not currently exist in any single Earth polity and would not exist for a minimum of eight to twelve years.
    34|
    35|*May be possible to dispatch small automated cargo deliveries within a six-to-eight year window, contingent on successful launch vehicle reconstruction and orbital logistics restoration. No commitment can be made at this time. Priority for all available launch capacity is Earth-internal infrastructure.*
    36|
    37|The phrase that stayed with Gabriel, that lodged somewhere between his ribs and his spine, was this one:
    38|
    39|*We love you. We have not forgotten you. We are building what we can. But we cannot build a fleet that reaches you. Not now. Perhaps not in our lifetimes.*
    40|
    41|He read it again. He read the lullaby from Reykjavik again. He sat in the comms room at 2140 hours on a Tuesday and understood, with the particular clarity that comes when waiting finally receives an answer, that the answer was *no* dressed in language kind enough to survive the three-hundred-million-kilometer journey.
    42|
    43|He could have transmitted everything immediately or waited until morning. He could have gone to Elena's quarters and given her the information first, as she deserved a private moment before the weight of it settled.
    44|
    45|He chose the third option.
    46|
    47|---
    48|
    49|## Scene 2
    50|
    51|Elena was awake. She was sitting at her table with a cup of something that smelled like roasted root tea -- she had stopped pretending it was coffee two years ago -- and she was reading one of Gabriel's archive printouts, which he gave her regularly so she could see how the colony's story was being told to a future she would not fully inhabit.
    52|
    53|He knocked. She opened the door on the second knock.
    54|
    55|*Second knock means she was expecting me,* he thought. *Or she is always awake and I am always expected.*
    56|
    57|"I need to talk to you."
    58|
    59|She saw his face and put the cup down. "Sit."
    60|
    61|He placed his tablet on her table and told her what the transmission contained. He did not soften it. He did not dramatize it. He told her the facts as they were: Earth was recovering but fractured, industrial capacity was partial, no fleet existed or was planned, there might be small automated deliveries in six to eight years if Earth's own reconstruction did not consume all available launch resources first.
    62|
    63|Elena listened without expression. Her face settled into the particular neutrality she had developed over fourteen years of receiving news and deciding, in real time, what the colony could bear. He had seen it on dozens of occasions. It was not absence of feeling. It was the controlled compression of feeling into a shape that could be used.
    64|
    65|She sat in silence for perhaps ninety seconds.
    66|
    67|Then she picked up her cup, found it empty, put it down, and said, "I already knew. Not the specifics. But the shape."
    68|
    69|Gabriel blinked. "You knew?"
    70|
    71|"Not with this level of detail. But I knew that if Earth could build a fleet, they would have told us by now. The signals we've received -- the gaps, the delays, the tone changes in the personal messages -- they're consistent with an industrial base that can send a letter but not a ship." She looked at him. "I've known for at least two years."
    72|
    73|"Then why --"
    74|
    75|"Because knowing something and announcing it to thirty-two families, including a woman who is six months into her first pregnancy and a workshop that finally has its first reliable output of local parts -- because announcing it means choosing the exact shape of the announcement." She touched the edge of her tablet. "You made the right call. You brought it to me first. Tomorrow, I'll decide how the colony hears this."
    76|
    77|"How will they hear it?"
    78|
    79|She looked out her small circular window, where outside the regolith-covered habitat wall blocked any view of the sky. But she looked through it, the way she always looked through windows that showed only dirt.
    80|
    81|"They'll hear it honestly. No softening. No dramatics. Just the facts and the recognition that the facts are what they are. Not worse. Not better." She turned back to him. "And then we go back to work. Because the work was never going to change."
    82|
    83|Gabriel nodded. He realized that Elena had not been waiting for the fleet. She had been waiting for Earth to stop pretending on the colony's behalf. The truth -- even the hard truth -- was cleaner than deferred hope.
    84|
    85|"And Elara?" he asked, naming the child who had been given Earth's sky as her middle name less than three hours ago. *Elara Aisling Varga-Naser.* A child of two worlds, one of which would never see her.
    86|
    87|Elena's expression changed. Just slightly. Just enough.
    88|
    89|"Elara is Martian," she said. "She always was. We just haven't told ourselves properly."
    90|
    91|Gabriel left her quarters at 2230 hours. She stood at the window a moment longer, then picked up her cup, looked at it again, and went to bed.
    92|
    93|He did not sleep. He returned to the comms room and listened to the Reykjavik lullaby three more times, thinking about the choir that sang it -- children on a world that still had oceans and weather and a sky that could be seen from the ground -- singing into a microphone for children they would never meet, on a planet they could not reach, in a future that belonged to Mars alone.
    94|
    95|The signal had taken fourteen minutes to cross the void. The distance had not changed. What had changed was the story the colony told itself about the other end of the wire.
    96|
    97|---
    98|
    99|## Scene 3
   100|
   101|Elena called the council to the meeting hall at 0700 the next morning. Not the full colony -- not yet. The council first: Arun, Laila, Mei, Tomas, Imani, Jonah, Gabriel. Seven people who had been making decisions together for so long that the word *council* felt almost quaint, an artifact of a formal structure laid over an informal habit.
   102|
   103|They arrived within five minutes of the broadcast. The meeting hall had been expanded twice since the original habitat days, most recently after the fire in Habitat Three, and it could now seat about sixty people comfortably. Today it held seven, which made it feel too large and too intimate at the same time.
   104|
   105|Elena stood at the front. She did not sit behind a desk or position herself as an authority delivering a briefing. She stood the way she always stood when truth needed to be told without ornament: feet planted, hands loose at her sides, eye contact distributed.
   106|
   107|"Earth sent a message last night," she began. "Full report is in your tablets. I'll summarize."
   108|
   109|She did. It took six minutes. Six minutes to compress fourteen months of quiet speculation into a statement of fact. When she was done, there was silence in the room. Not the heavy silence of shock. Not the tense silence of people waiting for bad news to continue. The particular silence of people hearing the last note of a song they had already recognized.
   110|
   111|Arun spoke first.
   112|
   113|"Industrial recovery is real. Six-to-eight year window for automated deliveries is plausible if the launch infrastructure stabilizes. No fleet." He looked at his hands. "The math we've been using for the last five years assumed no Earth resupply. That math is still correct. Nothing changes in our power budget, water projections, or food planning."
   114|
   115|Laila nodded. "Medical supply planning assumed no Earth resupply. Still correct. If automated deliveries arrive in six years, that's bonus inventory. If they arrive in eight, that's also bonus. We don't wait for either."
   116|
   117|Mei's contribution was shorter. "Seeds are local now. Three generations of selection. Earth couldn't send anything we need." She paused. "Except maybe more coffee beans. I'd accept those."
   118|
   119|Imani let out a sound -- not a laugh, not a sigh, something between them. "I stopped mapping supply routes from Earth two years ago. My maps are Martian. They always were."
   120|
   121|Jonah, characteristically, was the hardest to read. He sat with his arms crossed and his eyes fixed on a point somewhere between the table and infinity. After a long pause, he said, "I was born on a world where everything was imported and manufactured elsewhere. I built my whole identity on being a person who could make things from what we had. If Earth had announced a fleet, honestly? I would have been worried it would make us softer."
   122|
   123|Tomas, in his flat, precise way, said, "The robot fleet cannot be replaced. I have known this for four years. I have been preparing for it. Preparation means nothing changes today."
   124|
   125|The silence returned. Not dramatic. Not heavy. The particular silence of a group of people who had already survived the emotional work of this realization and were now simply confirming that survival had been genuine.
   126|
   127|Elena watched them -- these people who had not been chosen for stoicism but had developed it through repeated contact with a planet that did not care whether they lived -- and felt something she could not immediately name.
   128|
   129|Later, in her private log, she would call it *dignity*. But at the moment it felt more like release. The kind of release that comes when a weight you've been carrying isn't removed but is finally acknowledged as permanent, so the body stops bracing for it to change.
   130|
   131|Gabriel spoke last.
   132|
   133|"I've been thinking about what to write in the archive," he said. "Because every significant moment in the colony's history has an archive entry, and this is significant."
   134|
   135|"It is," Laila said. "It's the moment we stopped being a stranded mission and became something else entirely."
   136|
   137|"What's the something else?" Imani asked.
   138|
   139|"Permanent residents," Tomas said.
   140|
   141|"A city," Jonah said.
   142|
   143|"A civilization," Mei said quietly, surprised by the size of the word she'd chosen.
   144|
   145|Elena looked at them one at a time. Seven people. Seven faces that had aged visibly since landing. Seven people who had lost the person they were when they came here and become someone the person they were would barely recognize -- but someone they preferred, if asked honestly.

   147|"In the archive," Gabriel said, "I'm going to write that Earth answered the question we stopped asking. And the answer was what we already knew. And knowing it for certain didn't break us. Because we were already beyond the phase where breaking was an option."
   148|
   149|Elena nodded. "That's what I'd write."
   150|
   151|They discussed operational details for another twenty minutes -- communications protocols with Earth, whether to confirm receipt of the message, what Elena's reply would say, how to handle the personal letters that would need broadcasting to the colony at large.
   152|
   153|Then they stood. And they went to work.
   154|
   155|Nobody broke. Nobody needed to. The colony had survived a dust storm that blinded the surface for three weeks. It had survived a fire in a sealed habitat. It had survived the death of three colonists and the near-death of six more. It had survived the first birth, the first naming, the first year where every single calorie consumed had been grown, processed, or recycled locally.
   156|

   160|
   161|---
   162|
   163|## Scene 4
   164|
   165|Elena's quarters had very little personal decoration. She had never been a person who filled spaces with artifacts of who she was before. On Earth, she had a photograph of her parents on her desk and a shelf with books she hadn't yet finished reading. She had also had a uniform -- crisp, dark blue, with the mission patch on the left shoulder and rank insignia on the collar, carefully stored in a vacuum-sealed bag since Cycle 402. On Mars, textiles were too valuable to waste as display.
   166|
   167|She opened the storage locker in the corner. Inside: the uniform. Still sealed. Still pristine. A physical artifact of a version of herself who had believed that she was the commander of a mission that would one day go home.
   168|
   169|She unsealed the bag.
   170|
   171|The uniform came out smelling faintly of the preservative compound -- sharp, chemical, wrong. She shook it out and held it up in front of her. Dark blue. Earth blue. The color of a sky Mars did not have.
   172|
   173|She thought about the moment she had packed it. Cycle 402, the morning after the blackout, when she had looked around the damaged habitat and understood that *return* was no longer the default assumption.    174|
   175|Storage is a form of hope. Or at least the physical manifestation of not-yet-ready-to-let-go.
   176|
   177|She held the uniform for a long time. She considered putting it on. She was not sure why. Not for sentimentality -- she was not a sentimental person, or at least she had become someone for whom sentiment took forms other than clothing.    178|
   179|Perhaps she wanted to put it on as a form of closure -- the way a person visiting a grave might touch a stone and feel, for one moment, the shape of the thing they're losing.
   180|
   181|Instead, she folded it. Not the careful folding of someone storing something important. The looser folding of someone handling an artifact they are no longer obligated to protect.
   182|
   183|She placed it in the recycling bin.
   184|
   185|The bin was a simple device -- a thermal decomposition unit that broke down textiles into constituent fibers and compounds. The recycled material fed into the colony's fabrication stream.    186|
   187|She pressed the button. The bin hummed. In forty minutes, the dark blue fabric of a mission that would never go home would be transformed into something a Martian child would use to stay warm.
   188|
   189|She sat on the edge of her bed.
   190|
   191|For fourteen years, she had been Commander Elena Varga, leader of a mission that assumed -- always, underneath everything -- that one day a ship would come to take them home. She had carried that assumption not as a delusion but as a discipline.
   192|
   193|It had been wrong. Not wrong in a way that made her a fool. Wrong in the way all mission plans are wrong -- as simplified models of a reality that is larger and more permanent than the models allow.
   194|
   195|She released herself.
   196|
   197|It was not dramatic. She did not cry. She did not speak aloud. She did not have a vision or a revelation or a moment of cinematic transformation. She simply felt the weight she had been carrying shift its shape and then settle, and in that settling she experienced the particular quiet of someone who has set down a thing they no longer need.
   198|
   199|*Commander of a temporary mission* dissolved. What remained was something harder to name but easier to carry. Not a commander. Not yet. Something between a founder and a gardener -- someone who plants things not because she will harvest them but because planting is the work.

   202|
   203|*Cycle 1,972. Personal addendum. I have released myself from the identity of commander of a waiting mission. What I am now is not a title from Earth. It is a role Mars has asked me to fill.    206|
   207|It was an ordinary morning. That was the point. The most profound realignment of her identity, the quietest and most complete release she had ever experienced, and it did not change the temperature of her breakfast or the sound of the fans or the way the colony moved through its daily routines.
   208|
   209|A person who had broken under this news would have needed to make a scene. Elena did not. She had been doing it in pieces, over years, at times when the colony needed her to be steady.    210|
   211|She wondered if the uniform would really become a child's blanket padding. It probably would. A mission uniform becoming a child's comfort.
   212|

     3|*Mission AI: Cycle 1,452. I have completed a full integrity assessment of the colony's archival records. The hardware is functional. The storage media are intact.      5|---
     6|
     7|## Scene 1

     9|Gabriel found the error on a Thursday morning -- or what passed for Thursday on a planet that measured time in cycles and seasons rather than days of the week. Cycle 1,452.     11|The error was small -- a gap in the index for Cycles 1,280 through 1,295.     12|
    13|Gabriel found this on a Thursday morning -- or what passed for Thursday. Cycle 1,452. He had come to the archive terminal, as he did every few days, to cross-reference the Founding Record with Mission AI's raw logs.     15|He ran the integrity diagnostic on the full archive:
    16|
    17|ARCHIVE INTEGRITY ASSESSMENT -- CYCLE 1,452
    18|Total files: 47,213
    19|Files intact: 46,891
    20|Files with minor metadata errors: 289
    21|Files corrupted (unreadable): 33
    22|Index corruption affected: 1,156 files
    23|Index recovery possible: 867 files
    24|Index recovery impossible: 289 files

    29|
    30|"Mission AI," he said.
    31|
    32|The voice came through the corridor speaker -- quiet, measured, the voice that had been narrating the colony's existence since the moment the ships touched down. "I am aware of the integrity assessment results. I ran it this morning before you arrived."

    34|"Can you recover the index corruption? The full fifteen-cycle block? Cycle 1,280 through 1,295."

    36|"I can recover 867 of 1,156 affected files. The remaining 289 have metadata errors that prevent automated index reconstruction. The files themselves are readable, but I cannot determine their proper placement in the sequence without manual intervention. Which means --"

    81|

    84|He stopped recording. Not because he was done. Because he needed to find Elena before the day shifted and the crisis of the moment -- there was always a crisis of the moment -- pushed this conversation further down a list that it did not belong on.

    88|## Scene 2
    89|

    91|
    92|"Gabriel," she said, without looking up. "You have the face."
    93|
    94|"What face."
    95|
    96|"The face you had when you found the water extraction discrepancy in Cycle 900. The face you had when you learned the blackout logs were incomplete. The face you make right before you ask me to do something I don't want to do but should have done a year ago."

    99|

   103|
   104|"We have lost eighteen percent of the narrative coherence in our archive. Eighteen percent of the connective tissue. And public archive access -- everyone should be able to read the Founding Record, not just me and you and Mission AI."
   109|
   110|Elena was quiet, thinking the way she thought -- not about one thing but about everything the thing touched.
   111|
   112|"Labor hours," she said. "You're asking for -- twelve person-hours per week? Eight from the two archive workers, four from Mission AI."
   113|
   114|"Approximately."
   115|
   116|"Twelve hours not spent maintaining the bioloop. Not spent on repair or education or medical research or --"
   117|
   118|"Or any of the things that keep the colony alive," Gabriel finished. "But memory is infrastructure. If we forget our failures, we will repeat them with fewer excuses.
