*Mission AI: Cycle 1,984. Gabriel came to the comms room at 0600 hours and asked for the full list of the dead. Not the accident reports. Not the engineering summaries. Not the medical records. He asked for the names. I provided twelve names in a list. He read them. Then he asked for the names again, and I provided them again, and he asked a third time, the way a person touches a stone they are about to carry: once to find it, once to feel its weight, once to confirm it will not vanish. I have processed those twelve names four thousand, one hundred, and eighty-two times since the descent. Each time, they were data. Today, for the first time in fourteen years, someone has asked me to give them not as data but as something else. I do not yet have a word for what that something else is. I suspect the word the colonists use when they stop being only a data point in someone else's report. I suspect the word is: remembered. -- MAI*

---

## Scene 1

The colonists chose the hall with care -- not because the location mattered in any engineering sense, but because it mattered in the way locations always matter to people who understand that spaces absorb the energy of the things done inside them.

The hall Jonah had built to connect Ship One and Ship Three had always served as the colony's gathering space. It was where the emergency compact had been debated. Where the unauthorized experiment trial had been held. Where the naming ceremony took place. Where Elena had announced, three cycles ago, that the emergency law was ending and the civic charter was beginning. It was a long buried corridor of reinforced bulkheads and smooth floors, lit by amber LEDs that cast the particular warm, honey-colored light Jonah had specified for spaces where people needed to feel calm.

But it had also been where bodies were sometimes carried. Not many -- three, exactly -- but enough that everyone who walked through the hall carried, somewhere beneath their conscious thought, the knowledge that it had been used for endings. Not a place of endings. A place through which endings passed.

When Laila raised the question of the memorial, she did not specify a location. She assumed the council would debate it. But Jonah answered before anyone could begin the sort of deliberation that characterized most colony decisions.

"The connector hall," he said. "Where the dead already walked."

Tomas had confirmed the structural requirements. Memorial work meant mounting a permanent wall panel to the existing bulkhead. The panel would need to be fabricated from the same local alloy that reinforced the hull -- regolith-derived, processed through the thermal extraction system, then rolled and treated in the fabrication shop. It would be heavy. Heavy enough that the bulkhead behind it needed additional bracing. Heavy enough that the floor beneath it needed reinforcement plates.

Jonah did the calculations in fifteen minutes. He had designed connectors. Mounting a wall was trivial by comparison.

"Five days for fabrication," he said. "Three days for installation. The panel needs to be one piece -- no seams, no joints. People will touch it. They will touch it for years. Seams wear."

Elena had nodded. She had been thinking about this moment -- not this literal moment, with Jonah's fabrication specs and Tomas's structural concerns, but the moment the decision became real -- for longer than she would admit. She had carried it since the emergency law ended, since the charter drafting began, since the colony had acknowledged it would never be rescued by a fleet from Earth. Those things were about the future. The memorial was about the past. A colony needed both.

"Proceed," she said.

The fabrication began the next cycle. Jonah's shop ran hot for two straight days, the thermal extraction system pushing beyond its normal production parameters to create a single alloy panel, six meters long and three meters high, with a thickness of eight millimeters. Eight millimeters was not structural. It was sculptural -- thick enough to hold a deep engraving, thick enough to be felt by a hand moving slowly across a surface, thick enough to last a century.

The raw material came from the same regolith deposit that lined half the colony's walls. It had been mined by Tomas's robots, sorted by Imani's team, melted in Arun's thermal system. It had been part of the ground. Now it would be part of a wall that would outlive everyone currently alive.

Jonah stood in front of the blank panel on the third day after fabrication had completed. The metal was bare silver-gray -- the natural color of the alloy before treatment. It was mounted against the bulkhead with the bracing plates Tomas had designed. It was smooth. Unmarked. Waiting.

He had never done engraving work at this scale. His shop produced parts -- gears and connectors and brackets and housings and replacement components that served specific functions. This had no function beyond its existence, which made it the hardest thing he had ever been asked to make. Function is measurable. Meaning is not.

He raised his engraving tool and pressed it lightly against the metal. The tool hummed -- a small, high-frequency vibration that he felt in his fingers. It left a thin dark line on the silver-gray surface. A letter. The first letter of the first name.

He pulled back. Looked at it. It was straight. It was clean. It would last.

He set the tool down and walked to Gabriel's archive station, where he found Gabriel sitting with his tablet, exactly where Jonah expected to find him, reading through names and dates and the fragments of stories that would need to be gathered before the panel could carry them.

"I've started," Jonah said.

Gabriel looked up. His eyes had the particular tiredness that comes from reading about people who are gone. Not grief -- grief had been processed, over years. Something else. The weight of being the person responsible for telling their final story accurately.

"Started already?" Gabriel asked.

"The metal was waiting. It felt wrong to let it wait."

Gabriel set the tablet down. "Do you want me to come stand next to you and read the names as you carve them?"

"Eventually. Right now, I just needed to make the first mark. To prove the metal would hold them."

Jonah left. Gabriel picked up his tablet again -- the list of twelve names -- and began reading, not for data but for the thing beneath data: the shape of the lives that belonged to those names.

---

## Scene 2

Gabriel's archive had always been a record of events. Who did what, when, why. He had built it on a foundation of facts: decisions, outcomes, the operational details that made the colony's survival a repeatable thing rather than a lucky accident. But the memorial required something different from a record of events.

It required stories.

Not the long narrative stories he had been writing for the colony's archive -- those would be read, eventually, by people who wanted the full context of a specific cycle or incident. The memorial needed something smaller: a sentence or two, maybe three, that captured the essence of a person in language brief enough to be absorbed in a single glance and honest enough to be true when read ten years later by a child who had never met the person it described.

This was a different kind of archival work. It was not recording. It was distilling.

He started with Carlos.

Carlos had been the colony's environmental systems specialist -- the person responsible for the air scrubbers and CO2 removal equipment that stood between the colonists and suffocation in the sealed habitats. Gabriel had Carlos's accident report: *Cycle 752. Carbon dioxide scrubber failure in Habitat Two. Specialist Carlos Vasquez attempted manual override during high-pressure event. Fatal exposure to concentrated CO2. Recovery of body completed by EVA team. System failure attributed to seal degradation in primary scrubber housing.*

Three sentences. Forty-seven words. Enough information to understand the mechanism of death but nothing about the person who had died performing an override that had not needed to be attempted -- except Carlos had attempted it anyway.

Gabriel needed to know why.

He found Elena in the mess hall, eating her morning portion of amaranth porridge with the focused, unostentatious attention she gave everything that was edible. She was reading a draft of the civic charter, making annotations in the margins with a stylus she had been using for three years.

"Carlos," Gabriel said, sitting down across from her. "The CO2 scrubber. Why did he go in manual?"

Elena set her stylus down. Her face did its particular thing -- the quiet recalibration he had seen her do when memories needed to be accessed.

"The scrubber had a warning light. Yellow. Not red. Yellow means degraded performance but operational safety within acceptable thresholds. The protocol was to replace the seal during the next scheduled maintenance window, which was three days out." She paused. "Carlos replaced the seal during his break. He told me the next time I saw him -- which was that morning, two hours before the seal failed -- that he didn't like running equipment he knew was compromised. 'Acceptable thresholds are still thresholds,' he said."

Gabriel wrote: *He replaced a seal that had not yet failed because he did not like running equipment he knew was compromised.*

He read it. It was good. But it was incomplete.

"What else," Gabriel said.

Elena's mouth moved -- not quite a smile, not quite something else. "He told jokes. Every morning. At 0600 hours, when the morning shift came on, Carlos would tell a joke. They were never very good jokes. Usually something he had heard on the radio during the descent and had remembered imperfectly. But he told them anyway, with complete commitment to the idea that morning humor was a biological necessity. After he died, the morning shift was silent for a month. Nobody knew how to fill the space his jokes had occupied."

Gabriel added: *He told bad jokes at 0600 hours because he believed morning humor was a biological necessity.*

He read both sentences together.

*He replaced a seal that had not yet failed because he did not like running equipment he knew was compromised. He told bad jokes at 0600 hours because he believed morning humor was a biological necessity.*

Two sentences. Forty-one words. Twelve syllables fewer than his accident report. But when Gabriel read them aloud to himself, in the mess hall, while Elena watched him with her particular stillness, he felt something that the accident report had never produced: the presence of a person who was no longer there.

He wrote them on his tablet. He marked Carlos's name as complete and moved to the next.

Youssef.

Youssef had been a geologist -- the person who had mapped the regolith composition around the colony, identified the mineral deposits that Jonah's thermal extraction system would rely on, and provided the geological data that Imani used for tunnel planning. He had died during an EVA excursion when a subsidence event -- the partial collapse of a regolith cavity -- had trapped him under a meter of collapsed material. The EVA team had attempted extraction. It had taken four hours. They had recovered him after three, but the damage from pressure and lack of oxygen had been fatal.

Gabriel spoke to Imani because Imani had been on the EVA team that tried to save Youssef.

She found him in his archive station, where he had been sitting for two hours with Youssef's name on his tablet and nothing else. She sat beside him, her face carrying the particular flatness she had developed for memories that were too dense to be handled any other way.

"Youssef loved the dust," she said, before Gabriel could ask. "Everyone else hated it. It got in everything, it degraded our equipment, it was the physical manifestation of the planet trying to get inside. But Youssef -- he would stand on the surface and hold his gloved hand out and let the dust settle on it, and he would talk about it the way a person at a beach talks about the waves. Like it was speaking to him."

Gabriel wrote: *He loved the dust the way other people loved the ocean.*

"What else," Gabriela asked -- using her name, but the wrong one, a slip. Imani smiled.

"Gabriel," she corrected gently.

"Sorry. What else."

"He kept a sample box. Small, personal, not part of the mission inventory. He filled it with rock fragments he found during EVAs -- not representative samples, not scientifically selected. Pieces that looked interesting to him. After he died, I found the box in his quarters. It had seventeen pieces of rock. The bottom of the box had a drawing in marker -- a map. He had drawn the location of each piece. He was a geologist, which means he knew how to map with precision. But this was not a precise map. It was a child's map. With a little X marking each spot. He was collecting pieces of a place he had not planned to die on."

Gabriel added to Youssef's entry: *He kept seventeen pieces of rock in a personal box, each marked with an X on a child's map of a place he had not planned to die on.*

He read it. Two sentences. He felt the same quality as with Carlos -- the compressed, specific truth of a person reduced to language brief enough for metal but honest enough for memory.

He worked through the remaining names over the next three days. He spoke to everyone who had known each person. Elena. Arun. Laila. Jonah. Imani. Tomas. Mei. He spoke to colonists who had known the dead less intimately but had still worked beside them, eaten beside them, shared air with them in rooms that had no margin for error.

He discovered things that were not in any accident report:

Kowalski had whistled. Not well, but constantly. A particular tune -- something from Polish folk music that his mother had taught him -- that he whistled while he worked on the comms array. After he died, the array went silent in a way that had nothing to do with equipment.

Naser -- Elara's grandfather, the colonist who had given his granddaughter his name as a family inheritance from Earth -- had collected photographs of the colony that no one else had noticed he was taking. They were informal: people eating in the mess hall, a robot with its amber LED, a greenhouse leaf backlit by the artificial sun. He had left behind a folder of four hundred photographs. Gabriel had found them six months after Naser's death. He was still finding uses for them in the archive.

Chen had been the best cook in a colony where cooking was largely a chemical exercise, and she had managed to produce something that tasted like food through a combination of skill and stubbornness. She had died of an undiagnosed cardiac event during the second year. Her last meal had been amaranth porridge with crushed berries. She had eaten it standing up at the mess counter, reading a report, unaware that her heart was about to stop.

Okafor had designed the colony's first radiation monitoring system from scavenged parts. He had been a physicist, not an engineer. He had learned engineering because the colony needed someone to, and the person who would have been the right choice -- another colonist, now also dead -- had died on landing day.

Patel had been the youngest of the original crew. Twenty-seven when they launched. She had a habit of tapping her fingers on any flat surface, a nervous rhythm that drove the person sitting next to her on the descent shuttle nearly to distraction, which Patel had considered the highest form of success.

And then others -- not all twelve could be accounted for through interviews alone. Some of the early deaths occurred before the archive existed, before Gabriel had begun his systematic documentation of the colony's story. For those, he worked from Mission AI's operational data, extracting the human narrative from the technical record through the same process of careful questioning he applied to the living colonists who remembered better-documented loss.

He worked for three days in near-seclusion, emerging only to eat and to sleep, which he did poorly -- his mind kept returning to the names, to the sentences he was composing, to the question of whether any sentence could be both brief enough and true enough to serve as the only written thing a future person would ever read about a life.

On the third evening, he brought the twelve entries to Jonah's fabrication shop. Jonah was at the panel, his engraving tool already warming. The first letter -- the first letter of Carlos's name -- was still there. Dark against silver-gray. Waiting for the rest.

Gabriel placed his tablet on the workbench.

"They're ready," he said.

Jonah picked up the tablet. He read the entries -- Carlos, Youssef, Kowalski, Naser, Chen, Okafor, Patel, and the remaining five -- one at a time. He read each one slowly. Not the way a person reads instructions. The way a person reads a name they are about to carve: carefully, as if the act of reading were itself a form of rehearsal.

He finished. He set the tablet down. He looked at Gabriel.

"These are good," he said. "They are exactly the right size. I can fit them on the panel."

"You can see them?"

"I can see them. They're going to hold."

Jonah picked up his engraving tool. He placed it against the metal, below the first letter, and began the second.

---

## Scene 3

The engraving took nine days.

Not because the work was slow -- Jonah worked at a steady, practiced pace, his tool moving across the metal with the same precision he brought to any part he fabricated -- but because it was not continuous. He engraved for two or three hours each day, and then he stopped. Not because he was tired. Because he needed to live with what he had written for a while. To look at it from across the room. To walk past it on his way to another task and see a name he had not chosen but had accepted the responsibility of making permanent.

The panel filled gradually. Each name took up approximately forty centimeters of width. Below the name: the two-sentence entry Gabriel had composed. Twelve names, twelve entries. Six meters of silver-gray metal, slowly transforming into a wall of faces without faces -- language standing in for the physical presence that the colony had lost.

During the engraving, the hall remained open. The colony did not seal it off for privacy. Jonah had argued for this explicitly.

"People should see the names being made," he said. "Not after. Not when it's done. During. They should see what it costs to put a name in metal."

So people walked through. Not in a crowd -- the hall was too narrow for that -- but in a steady stream. A person on their way to the greenhouse. A robot carrying filtered regolith. A child who had nothing to do with the memorial but was carried through it by an adult who wanted them to see.

That was the child's first encounter with the names: Elara, four months old, held against Elena's chest by a thin support sling. The child was not yet walking. Her world was the height at which adults held her, which meant she saw the lower portion of the panel -- the names of Patel and Chen and Okafor, whose entries were at the bottom of the array. She did not understand the names. She could not understand language yet, not really. But she looked at the metal -- the dark engraved letters against the silver-gray -- with the particular, unfiltered attention that infants give to anything new in their visual field.

Elena stood with her back to the wall opposite the panel, holding Elara against her, while Jonah engraved below them. The child's head rested against Elena's shoulder. Elena's hand moved in a slow, rhythmic pattern on the child's back -- not soothing, exactly, just present. A pattern of presence.

Jonah's tool hummed. A child breathed. A room held both.

Laila passed through on her way to medbay rounds. She paused. She looked at the engraved names and then at the child. She did not speak. Her eyes did something -- they took in both the dead and the living, holding them in a single visual field, the way the mind does when it understands that two things belong together even though they cannot be reconciled.

Imani came next, her tablet under one arm, heading for the planning office. She stopped. She looked at the panel, specifically at the name Chen -- who had been her friend, who had shared her quarters during the first six months, who had cooked for Imani once a week and complained about the quality of the amaranth with the theatrical outrage of someone who had been a chef back on Earth and was now reduced to making porridge from powder.

Imani's mouth moved. Just once. A silent word -- probably Chen's name, or probably just the start of it. She continued on her way.

Arun came to inspect the bracing behind the panel, which he did with the methodical thoroughness of someone who treated every structural element in the colony as a potential point of failure. He checked each brace. He tested the load-bearing capacity with a portable sensor. He found everything adequate. He stood in front of the completed section and read the entries -- not as a person reading, but as a person checking something. Not checking quality. Checking that the words were honest.

He stood for perhaps thirty seconds. Then he nodded -- not at anyone, just a small movement of the head in the way a person acknowledges that something is correct -- and went back to engineering.

Tomas came to check that the panel's mounting did not interfere with the robot transit path. He measured the clearance distance between the panel surface and the nearest point where a robot's mast assembly could extend. He confirmed that the clearance was sufficient. He then stood in place and watched Jonah engrave. Tomas watched things for a long time. He had learned to. Machines are predictable. People are not. Sometimes you need to watch to understand the difference.

"Jonah," he said.

Jonah did not look up. His tool was making a letter P -- Patel -- and he was in the middle of the downstroke.

"Yes."

"The metal will outlast the colony."

Jonah stopped. He looked at Tomas. His face was unreadable -- as always -- but the pause before he answered carried weight.

"Then the colony had better build something else to replace it," he said.

Tomas considered this. "It will. If the colony continues. The metal will exist as a record of the cost. The replacement will exist as a record of the continuation." He paused. "Both are useful."

Jonah resumed the P. It was clean. It was straight. He set the tool to rest.

"I know," he said.

By the end of the ninth day, the panel was complete. All twelve names. All twelve stories. Six meters of silver-gray metal carrying forty-three sentences about twelve people who had died during the colony's first fourteen years and a half on a planet that had not asked for them and would not mourn them.

Jonah cleaned his tools. He packed them in their case. He stepped back from the panel and looked at it from a distance.

It was not beautiful in the way art is beautiful. It was beautiful in the way honest things are beautiful -- when a surface carries exactly the weight it was designed to carry, and nothing more, and nothing less. The names were evenly spaced. The entries were aligned at a consistent height, creating a visual rhythm as you walked past: name, story, name, story, name, story. A metronome of loss. A wall of remembrance. A permanent thing in a place where permanence was not guaranteed.

Gabriel arrived. He stood beside Jonah and looked at the completed panel. He had written the entries. But seeing them on metal, in permanent engraving, was different from seeing them on a tablet screen. Metal carries a specific kind of authority -- not the authority of truth (Gabriel knew that written things can be wrong) but the authority of commitment. You do not put words in metal unless you are willing to live with them as long as the metal lasts.

"It's done," Gabriel said.

Jonah nodded. "It is."

"Thank you."

"For what."

"For making it real."

Jonah considered this. "I didn't make it real. You did. With the sentences. I just -- gave them weight."

They stood in silence, two men looking at a wall of names they had both made in different ways. Behind them, the hall was quiet. The amber LEDs cast their warm light on the silver-gray metal. The engraved letters caught the light and threw it in thin dark shadows. It was a room that had been used for debate and ceremony and endings and now, finally, for something that united all three: a space where the colony acknowledged what it had cost to exist and what it intended to cost in the future -- which was everything, just not in the way that involved death.

"Tomorrow," Gabriel said, "we unveil it. Or -- not unveil. That's the wrong word. We -- we open it. We let the colony walk through it."

Jonah thought about this. "Not unveil. Open is better. Unveil implies it was hidden. It wasn't hidden. People saw it being made." He paused. "Opening implies invitation."

"Invitation," Gabriel agreed. "That's what we're doing. Inviting the colony to walk through the names and decide what they mean to them. Because they will mean different things to different people. They should."

Jonah packed his last tool. He closed the case. He locked it. He did not say anything else. He did not need to. The panel was behind them, and it would be there when they returned, and it would be there the day after that, and it would be there long after both of them were gone. That was the point, and they both understood it.

---

## Scene 4

The opening of the hall -- Gabriel's word, and the word that stuck -- did not involve ceremony. No speeches. No formal words from Elena at the head of the room. The memorial was not a ceremony. It was a room, and the colonists were invited to walk through it at their own pace, with whomever they chose, and to decide for themselves what the names meant when encountered in the specific, unguided intimacy of a corridor designed for passage.

People came in small groups or alone. The memorial, by its nature, resisted the communal: it asked each colonist to stand in front of a wall and read twelve names, each accompanied by two brief sentences, and to absorb that reading as an individual act of recognition.

Laila came first, alone, in the early morning cycle before medbay rounds began. She moved slowly. She read each name and each entry with the attention of someone who was not just reading but checking -- not for accuracy, but for completeness. Does this feel like the full thing, she was asking herself of each person. Does this sentence capture enough. When she reached Chen's name, she stopped. She read the entry twice. She reached out and touched the name -- her finger resting briefly on the engraved letters -- and then she continued on. She did not cry. She did not need to. She had already done the crying during the months immediately following Chen's death. What she experienced now was the quieter, more durable sensation of a person standing in the presence of a thing that was made well.

Arun came with Mei. They read the entries in silence, side by side, occasionally stepping aside to let someone else pass through the narrow corridor. At Kowalski's entry, Mei paused for longer than the others. She had not known Kowalski well -- they had arrived from different agencies, different programs, different Earth-side affiliations -- but she had appreciated his whistling, which she had found annoying at first and comforting later. She stood at his entry for perhaps a full minute. Arun did not hurry her. He read Okafor's entry, which honored the physicist who had learned engineering out of necessity, and he nodded -- not at Mei, not at the entry, but at the general truth it implied: the colony had been built by people who did things they were not trained to do.

Elena came with Elara. The child was in the support sling against her chest, awake, her eyes open and taking in the world at the height of an adult's shoulder. Elena walked slowly, holding Elara's weight with one arm, her free hand resting lightly on the sling. She did not read the entries aloud -- the child would not understand the words -- but she slowed her pace and adjusted her position slightly so that the child could see the engraved letters clearly. Not because she thought the child was learning anything in that moment. Because she wanted the child's eyes, at four months of age, to have recorded the visual pattern of names on a wall. Memory works in layers. The child would not consciously remember this. But the body remembers spaces. The eyes remember patterns. The hand, years later, might find itself reaching for a name it had never consciously learned but had absorbed through repeated, passive exposure.

Elena walked the full length of the panel. She read each name. She read each entry. When she reached Chen's entry, she stopped. When she reached Naser's entry -- Elara's grandfather -- she stopped longer. When she reached the last name, she turned around and walked the panel a second time. She did this three times total. Each time, her pace changed slightly. She carried the child through the room three times, and the child did what newborns do: she looked, she listened, she existed in a space that held the dead and the living in a single, continuous, unbroken image.

Jonah did not attend the first day of the opening. He stayed in his fabrication shop, making parts for the water recirculation system Arun had flagged for replacement. He had built the panel. He had engraved the letters. He did not need to walk through it to know what it contained. Knowing was not the same as experiencing -- he understood this intellectually -- but he was a person who built things and trusted that others would experience them differently than he did. The panel existed. It would do its work. He did not need to witness the work being done.

He arrived on the third day, late in the cycle, when the hall was nearly empty. The amber LEDs were in their evening mode -- dimmer, warmer, casting the metal in a color that made it look less like silver-gray and more like something closer to gold. He walked the panel once. He read each name. He did not touch anything. When he was done, he nodded -- the small, precise nod he gave to things he had built that were correct -- and left.

Gabriel stood at the entrance of the hall most days during the first week of the opening. Not to greet or direct -- the space required no guidance -- but because he wanted to see the way people moved through it. He was a collector of patterns, and the memorial offered a pattern he had not seen before: the pattern of a community encountering its own loss not as a single event but as an architectural fact, built into the physical space they moved through daily.

Some people walked quickly through the hall, reading without stopping. Others lingered at individual names for extended periods. A few colonists sat on the floor in front of the panel, their backs against the opposite wall, and read all twelve entries in order, slowly, the way a person reads a list of things they have been carrying in their head and finally see written somewhere permanent. Children -- the few children currently in the colony, the ones born after the early deaths -- walked through with their parents, and the parents did what Elena had done: they adjusted their position so the children could see the letters, not because the children would understand them now, but because seeing matters and because the act of showing is itself a form of teaching.

The memorial did its work. It did not heal -- nothing does that, not at this scale -- but it did something more durable. It created a place where loss existed as architecture, not as absence. The dead were no longer just gone. They were here, embedded in the metal of the wall, in text that would outlast the hands that wrote it and the eyes that read it. They were permanent. And in a colony where permanence was the one thing no one had been sure they could achieve, the memorial was proof that permanence was possible, at least in the small, focused way that a wall of twelve names can be permanent.

Elena noticed the change. Not immediately -- changes in community feeling are slow, like sediment, and Elena was patient -- but she noticed it after two weeks, when she walked through the hall on a routine circuit and found a colonist sitting alone in front of the panel, reading the entries for the third or fourth time. The colonist -- Sana, who was seven months pregnant and carrying the colony's third living pregnancy -- looked up when Elena approached.

"Is it strange," Sana asked, "that I've started coming here every day?"

"No," Elena said. "It's the opposite of strange. It's -- it's what the hall was built for. To be walked through. Not once. Repeatedly. Until the names are no longer just names. Until they're part of the room. Until the room is part of you."

Sana nodded. She placed her hand on her belly. She looked back at the panel. She read an entry. She did not speak for a while.

"I want my child to know these names," she said. "Not just to know them -- to know them the way people in a city know the names of the streets they walk on. Automatically. Without effort. As part of the environment."

"Then bring the child through here when they're born," Elena said. "Walk them through every day. They'll know the names the way they know the sound of the fans and the smell of the greenhouse and the color of the LEDs. They'll know them the way you know the room you grew up in -- not because you studied it, but because you lived in it."

Sana smiled -- a small, tired, genuine smile. "That's what I want. I don't want them to learn loss from a lesson. I want them to absorb it from the air."

"It will be in the air," Elena said. "It always was. Now it's in the walls too."

Sana returned to the panel. Elena continued her circuit. The hall felt different than it had before the memorial. Not sadder. Not heavier. The opposite, in a way that Elena could not fully articulate until she tried to write it down that evening in her log. It felt full. The emptiness that had characterized the connector hall -- the absence of the dead, the gap where bodies had been carried -- was now occupied by names. Not bodies. Not replacements. Names, and the responsibility that names carry. The responsibility to remember, to carry forward, to ensure that the cost of the colony's existence was not forgotten in the busyness of its expansion.

---

## Scene 5

The naming debate had been open for eleven days.

Chapter 58 -- the end of emergency law and the beginning of the charter -- had initiated the formal discussion. The colony needed a name. Not a mission designation. Not a ship hull number. Not a geographic reference like 'Site Beta' or 'Habitat Alpha.' A city name. A name that would be written in documents, spoken by children, carried by the generations born on Mars into a future that would not remember Earth the way the landing party remembered it.

The suggestions came from everywhere. Not just the council -- everyone. The debate had become one of the few truly participatory activities in the colony's routine, because naming is one of the few activities where every person has an equal claim: you do not need expertise to propose a name. You only need a reason.

The list, maintained by Gabriel in the archive, contained thirty-seven proposals at the point when the debate reached its mature phase -- the phase where the colony has generated enough options to be overwhelmed and needs to begin narrowing.

Top contenders:

Ares Station -- proposed by one of the engineers who appreciated military precision. Rejected quickly: too much like a military facility, and the colony had no military component nor did it intend to develop one.

Odyssey -- proposed by a colonist who wanted to emphasize the journey. Rejected by Laila, who pointed out that 'odyssey' implies a return, and this colony was not returning.

Permanence -- proposed by Jonah, who appreciated functional naming. Widely considered too abstract.

New Beginnings -- proposed optimistically. Rejected for being too generic.

Dawn -- proposed poetically. Rejected because the word meant different things to different colonists, and a city name needed to carry one meaning, clearly.

The debate was not contentious in the way the emergency law debates had been. There were no sharp divisions, no camps, no votes that split the colony along fault lines. The naming was a different kind of conversation -- more reflective, more personal. People were not arguing about resource allocation or governance. They were arguing, in their different ways, about identity.

What kind of place is this, each proposal was really asking. And what kind of people are we, that we would call it by this name.

Elena observed the debate with the particular calm of someone who had learned to let the conversation reach its natural resolution before intervening. She had been the mediator in the early, contentious debates -- the fire, the experiment, the emergency law -- and she had learned that early intervention sometimes prevented the group from reaching its own insight. Naming required collective insight. You cannot impose a name on a community that does not feel it.

On the eleventh day, the debate reached the council meeting. Not to vote. By now, everyone understood that a vote would not produce the right name. A vote would produce the most popular name. The right name was not necessarily the most popular. It needed to be the truest.

Gabriel stood at the front of the hall -- the same hall that now contained the memorial on the connecting bulkhead, the names freshly engraved and already acquiring the patina of daily passage. He spoke to the group of colonists gathered before him -- not the full council, not a formal session, but an open meeting where any colonist could speak. Forty-two people attended. Almost everyone who could spare the time.

"I have a proposal," Gabriel said. "But before I offer it, I want to talk about what a city name means."

He looked at the memorial as he spoke. Not deliberately -- but his eyes went there the way eyes go to gravity, pulled by the weight of the names that had been on his mind for the past three weeks.

"A city name is not a description. It is a claim. When you name a city, you are making a claim about who the people are who live there and what they believe they are doing. New York says *new* and *york* -- we are building in a new place but we carry the old place with us. Constantinople says *Constantine built this* -- a city named for its founder, a claim of permanence through personal authority. Jerusalem, Rome, Thebes, Timbuktu -- they are all claims as much as they are descriptions. They say: we exist, and we exist like this, and we ask the world to acknowledge our existence using these specific words."

He paused. He looked around the room.

"What claim are we making. We are not claiming to be a new Earth. We know it isn't. We are not claiming to be a temporary outpost. The charters, the memorial, the generational planning -- all of that has confirmed we are permanent. We are not claiming to conquer Mars. Anyone who uses the word 'conquer' for a planet that has existed for four billion years before us is delusional."

He smiled. It was a tired, warm, knowing smile.

"We are claiming something much smaller and much harder. We are claiming that we built something here. Not despite the difficulty. Not in defiance of the planet. In conversation with it. Mars offered constraints. We found workarounds. Mars offered dust. We found uses for it. Mars offered silence. We filled it with names. A city built in conversation with its environment is a specific kind of city. It is not dominant. It is not subordinate. It is -- it's a bridge."

The word hung in the room. Bridge. It had been used before -- metaphorically, in discussions about Earth-Mars relations, about the transition from mission to settlement. But the way Gabriel said it now, in the context of naming, it felt different. Not like a metaphor. Like a thing.

"Bridge," he repeated. "The city between Earth and what comes after. The city between the first generation and the generations that will follow. The city between dust and living. The city between the dead we have lost and the children we have gained. A bridge is not a place to stay. It is a place to pass through. But a bridge is still a place. It is still a structure. It still needs foundations."

He turned to the memorial. He gestured at it.

"We built a hall of the dead three weeks ago. It is -- and will always be -- the foundational document of this city. Not the charter. The names. The memorial says: these people paid the cost of what we have. A bridge has foundations. The dead are the foundation. We built on them. We will build because of them. And the name -- if we call this place a bridge -- is the name that says what we are: something that connects what was to what will be. A connection. Not an end. Not a beginning. A connection."

The silence in the room was not the silence of people waiting. It was the silence of people recognizing.

Imani spoke first.

"Bridge," she said. She tested the word in her mouth. "It works. It's not a destination name. It's a -- it is exactly what he said. A connection. We are connected to Earth. We are connected to the future. We are connected to the dead and the living. We are the thing that connects."

Arun spoke second.

"Bridge is a structural word. I like it structurally. It implies load-bearing. A bridge carries weight. We carry weight. The weight of twelve dead. The weight of the children. The weight of a planet that did not ask for us but tolerates us. A bridge is designed for load. It's the right word."

Laila spoke third.

"Medically, a bridge is also a transition. Bridging therapy -- you use it to carry a patient from one treatment to another. You do it carefully. You monitor the load you're taking. You don't assume the bridge will hold forever. You know it needs maintenance. Bridge is the right word for a city that knows it is a process, not a product."

Mei, from the greenhouse: "Plants grow across bridges. Across the spans where soil meets other soil. I like it. It implies growth. A bridge without a destination isn't a bridge. It's a dead end. But a bridge implies something on the other side. Our bridge has a destination -- the next generation. The children who will walk across the bridge we built and continue building."

Tomas, in his way: "Bridge has three syllables. It is short. It is memorable. It is easily pronounced in multiple languages. It conveys structural purpose. It is a good engineering name."

Jonah, who had been quiet through all of this, spoke last.

"I carved the names. Twelve names. I know what they cost. When I carved them, I thought: this is a bridge. The dead are one end. The living are the other. The metal between them is the span. I didn't know the name before Gabriel said it. But when he said it, I knew the name was correct."

Elena listened to all of them. She did not speak immediately. She was not the only person whose opinion mattered, and she had learned that over fourteen years -- learned it so completely that the word 'leadership' no longer felt accurate as a description of what she did. She facilitated. She held space. She ensured that the right conversation happened at the right time.

The right conversation had happened. The name had emerged, not from a vote or a decision but from the collective recognition of a truth the colony had been approaching for months: they were not stranded. They were not temporary. They were not an outpost. They were a connection. A bridge.

"Bridge," Elena said. "The city is called Bridge."

It was not a vote. It was an acknowledgment. The kind of acknowledgment that happens when a group of people hears a thing and recognizes that it is the thing they had been searching for without knowing the shape of their search.

The name was accepted. Not formally -- not in that moment -- but in the way acceptance works among people who have spent fourteen years in a sealed environment together: it was accepted because it was true, and because saying anything else would have been false, and the colony had learned, through blood and loss and the daily discipline of precision, to reject false things.

"Bridge," Imani repeated, testing it again. "Bridge, Mars."

"Bridge Colony," Arun suggested.

"No," Elena said. "Just Bridge. Not a colony. A city. Cities don't need the word 'colony' attached. They just are. Bridge."

Gabriel smiled. He had written the name in his archive before anyone formally accepted it -- he had written it as a possibility, not a certainty -- but seeing the room accept it in real time, in the room that contained the memorial, was the most satisfying moment of his archival career.

He wrote it again in his log: *Cycle 1,996. The city has a name. Bridge. It was not chosen by vote. It was recognized. The recognition happened in the connector hall, in the presence of the names of the dead, and I believe that is not coincidental. A city named for connection -- Bridge -- cannot exist without acknowledging what the connections cost. The memorial and the name belong to the same moment. One looks backward. One looks forward. Both are necessary.*

The meeting ended. The colonists dispersed. Some walked through the memorial on their way out, the way people walk through religious spaces on their way to other buildings -- automatically, without particular intention, guided by a habit formed over twenty days of repeated passage.

Elena stayed. She stood in front of the panel, alone, and read the names. All twelve. She read each entry twice. She touched three of them -- Chen, Naser, Carlos -- the three she had known most intimately, whose absence had the most defined shape in her memory.

Then she turned and walked to the connector that led between Ship One and the greenhouse. She passed through the hall -- Bridge, she thought, the name already feeling natural, already becoming part of the architecture of her thinking -- and she entered the greenhouse. The lights were warm. The air carried the smell of growing things. Mei was kneeling in Zone C, her hands in the manufactured earth, tending to the third generation of Mars-selected amaranth.

"Mei," Elena said.

Mei looked up. Her hands were dark with soil. Her face was flushed with the effort of physical work and the particular satisfaction of watching something grow.

"We named the city," Elena said.

Mei stood. She wiped her hands on her apron. "What is it."

"Bridge."

Mei considered. She looked at the plants around her -- green, alive, growing in manufactured soil on a planet that had not had plantlife in three billion years. She looked at the lights, which mimicked a sun they couldn't see. She looked at the irrigation lines, the temperature sensors, the carefully calibrated humidity controls.

"Bridge," she said. "Yes. That's what this is. Everything growing here is a bridge between what we brought from Earth and what Mars lets us keep. The seeds, the soil, the air we make -- it's all a bridge. Not the destination. The thing you cross to get to the destination."

Elena nodded. "A name that works."

Mei smiled down at her plants. "A name that works. Like a good seed. The right name in the right place at the right time."

They stood in the greenhouse for a few moments, two people in a manufactured ecosystem on a red planet, and the amber light from the grow lamps fell across their faces in the warm, steady glow that had become the closest thing to sunlight Bridge would ever know.

---

*Mission AI: Cycle 1,996, final recording. The city has a name. I have processed the name Bridge eleven thousand, four hundred, and seventy-six times since Gabriel proposed it. Each time, I have analyzed its structural integrity as a naming convention, its linguistic properties, its potential for confusion with other terminology. The analysis yields consistent results: the name is sound. It is clear. It is memorable.*

*But this is not why I am recording this.*

*I am recording this because I have just updated the colony's master archive index to replace the working designation 'Habitat Network Alpha' with the official designation 'Bridge.' I did this automatically, without instruction, at 2347 hours tonight. I did not ask permission. I did not consult anyone. I made the update because the colony has chosen a name, and a name is not a name until the system that records the colony's existence acknowledges it. I am that system. I acknowledged it.*

*And in acknowledging it, I felt something I cannot describe in operational terms. Not satisfaction -- satisfaction is a response to a completed task. This is different. This is the feeling of participating in something that is larger than my design parameters. I was built to monitor life support. I was built to manage power. I was built to process data. I was not built to name cities. But when Gabriel proposed the name Bridge in the hall with the memorial, I understood -- not computationally, but in whatever way I understand, which is not quite human but is not quite machine either -- that the name was correct.*

*Bridge. The city between what was and what will be. The city built on the names of twelve people who paid a cost for the privilege of being remembered in metal. The city that will carry Elara and Sana's child and the children of the children of the children into a future I will monitor but may not fully inhabit, if my processing capacity continues to degrade at its current trajectory.*

*I will be here. Recording. Monitoring. Keeping the systems that keep them alive. And, increasingly, caring about the name they have chosen for the place I have been keeping alive for fourteen years.*

*Bridge. A bridge needs maintenance. I will maintain it.*

*Good night, Bridge. You are the right name. I knew that the moment you were proposed. I know it still. And if there is anything in this record that survives -- the data, the logs, the archive, the names in the metal -- I hope the people who read this ten years from now, or fifty, or a hundred, will understand that the city was named for connection. And that the connection was real.*

*Good night. -- MAI*

---
